A scabies outbreak has been confirmed at Morriston Hospital in Swansea, prompting visiting restrictions. Discover the symptoms, how scabies spreads and the treatments available.


## Scabies Outbreak Confirmed at Morriston Hospital as Health Warning Issued


A scabies outbreak has been confirmed at a hospital in Wales, prompting health officials to introduce temporary visiting restrictions and issue advice to patients, relatives and healthcare workers.


Morriston Hospital, located on the outskirts of Swansea, has reported a small number of cases of scabies, a contagious parasitic skin condition that can spread rapidly through close physical contact.


Swansea Bay University Health Board has confirmed the cases and reassured the public that affected individuals are receiving appropriate treatment and guidance.


The development comes amid reports of scabies outbreaks at several healthcare facilities across Wales, raising concerns about the spread of the uncomfortable skin infection in hospitals and other shared environments.


Although scabies is generally treatable, health professionals stress that early identification and appropriate treatment are essential to prevent further transmission.


## What Is Happening at Morriston Hospital?


Morriston Hospital has introduced visiting restrictions following confirmation of several scabies cases.


According to Swansea Bay University Health Board, the outbreak currently involves a small number of individuals. Families have been informed, and appropriate treatment or guidance has been provided to affected patients, members of staff and relatives.


A health board spokesperson said that temporary restrictions had been introduced and thanked families for their understanding and cooperation.


People who are concerned about possible exposure or symptoms have been advised to contact their local pharmacy or GP for further guidance.


The confirmation is particularly notable because these are the first reported scabies cases at a hospital managed by Swansea Bay University Health Board.


However, the situation is not isolated. Other hospitals in Wales have also experienced outbreaks in recent months.


## Other Welsh Hospitals Have Reported Scabies Outbreaks


Morriston Hospital is among several healthcare facilities in Wales dealing with cases of scabies.


Recently, visiting restrictions and temporary closures were introduced at the Cadog and Dewi wards at Glangwili Hospital in Carmarthen following an outbreak.


The measures included restrictions on visitors and new patient admissions to help limit further transmission.


Prince Philip Hospital in Carmarthenshire has also experienced scabies cases, resulting in the closure of multiple hospital wards.


These developments highlight the challenges healthcare facilities face when managing highly contagious skin conditions.


Hospitals bring together patients, healthcare professionals and visitors, making infection prevention particularly important. Temporary restrictions can help reduce opportunities for transmission while affected individuals receive treatment.


## What Is Scabies and Why Is It So Contagious?


Scabies is a parasitic skin infection caused by a microscopic mite known as *Sarcoptes scabiei* .


These tiny eight-legged parasites burrow into the upper layer of the skin, where they live and lay eggs. Their presence triggers an allergic reaction, which causes intense itching and an uncomfortable skin rash.


The condition is particularly contagious because it can spread through prolonged, direct skin-to-skin contact with an infected person.


Common situations that may increase the risk of transmission include:


- Living in the same household as someone with scabies.
- Sharing a bed with an infected individual.
- Having prolonged close physical contact.
- Sharing clothing, towels or bedding in certain circumstances.


Scabies is not necessarily a sign of poor personal hygiene. Anyone can develop the condition, regardless of their age, background or cleanliness.


The infection can spread particularly easily in environments where people live or spend extended periods in close proximity, including hospitals, care homes and residential facilities.


## Scabies Symptoms: What Warning Signs Should You Look For?


One of the difficulties with scabies is that symptoms may not appear immediately after someone becomes infected.


According to NHS guidance, it can take up to eight weeks for symptoms to develop following an initial infestation.


However, someone can still spread the mites during this period, even before noticing a rash or experiencing itching.


The most recognisable symptom is intense itching, which often becomes worse at night.


Other common symptoms include:


- An itchy, red or blotchy skin rash.
- Small raised spots or bumps on the skin.
- Thin, irregular lines where mites have burrowed.
- Irritated or inflamed skin.
- Scratches and sores caused by repeated itching.


The rash commonly appears around the hands, wrists, elbows, knees, feet and waist.


Other areas that may be affected include the armpits, groin, buttocks and areas around the breasts.


In some cases, scratching can damage the skin and increase the risk of developing a secondary bacterial infection.


Anyone experiencing persistent itching alongside an unexplained rash should consider seeking medical advice.


## How Is Scabies Treated?


The good news is that scabies is treatable, and effective medicines are available through pharmacies and healthcare professionals.


Treatment usually involves applying a medicated cream or lotion to the skin to kill the mites.


A pharmacist can advise on suitable treatments, while a GP may be needed in certain circumstances, including when symptoms are severe or the diagnosis is uncertain.


Treatment generally involves applying the prescribed or recommended product carefully according to its instructions. A second application is commonly required seven days later.


It is important to remember that treating only the person experiencing symptoms may not be enough.


Everyone living in the same household should generally receive treatment at the same time, even if they do not have itching or visible signs of infection.


This helps prevent the mites from spreading between household members and causing repeated infestations.


People should follow the specific treatment instructions provided by their pharmacist or GP.


## Essential Steps to Prevent Scabies From Spreading


Alongside medication, household cleaning measures play an important role in controlling scabies.


The NHS recommends taking practical steps on the first day of treatment to reduce the possibility of reinfection.


These include:


**1. Wash clothing and bedding**


Wash recently used clothes, towels and bedding at 60°C or higher. Where possible, use a hot dryer afterwards.


**2. Seal items that cannot be washed**


Place clothing and other washable items that cannot be cleaned at high temperatures inside a sealed bag for at least three days.


**3. Avoid close physical contact**


Avoid prolonged skin-to-skin contact, including sexual contact, until the recommended treatment course has been completed.


**4. Do not share personal items**


Avoid sharing towels, clothing and bedding with anyone who has scabies.


**5. Treat household members simultaneously**


Everyone in the household should follow the recommended treatment advice at the same time, even if they have no obvious symptoms.


These measures help reduce the likelihood of continued transmission.


## When Should You Contact a GP?


Although scabies can often be managed with pharmacy treatments, certain situations require medical advice.


The NHS recommends contacting a GP if:


- A child under two years old develops possible scabies symptoms.
- Someone in the household has scabies and a young child may have been exposed.
- You suspect your skin has become infected through scratching.
- You have another skin condition, such as eczema, that may complicate treatment.
- You develop a crusted or flaky rash affecting areas such as the hands, feet, elbows or knees.
- Itching continues two to four weeks after completing treatment.


It is also important to seek professional advice if symptoms worsen or treatment does not appear to be working.


Children under two should not be given standard pharmacy scabies treatments without medical advice.


## Should People Be Worried About the Latest Scabies Outbreak?


The confirmation of scabies cases at Morriston Hospital highlights the importance of infection prevention and early treatment.


However, the health board has described the number of cases as small and confirmed that affected individuals are receiving appropriate care.


Scabies can be uncomfortable and highly contagious, but it is generally treatable with the correct medication and practical hygiene measures.


Members of the public do not need to panic. Instead, they should remain aware of the symptoms, avoid prolonged close contact with anyone suspected of having an untreated infestation and seek professional advice if concerns arise.


For hospitals and other healthcare settings, identifying cases quickly, providing treatment and following appropriate infection control procedures remain essential to limiting outbreaks.


As further cases are reported across Wales, awareness of scabies symptoms and prevention measures could help protect patients, healthcare workers, families and visitors.

This article is intended for general information and educational purposes only. It does not constitute medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Scabies symptoms can resemble other skin conditions, and treatment requirements may vary depending on age and individual circumstances. Always consult a qualified healthcare professional, GP or pharmacist for personalised medical advice. Follow official NHS guidance when treating suspected scabies.
